newsitem.title: USA: Humor no laughing matter to U.S. medicine.
newsitem.headline: Humor no laughing matter to U.S. medicine.

text.p: There are many scientific conferences in Orlando, but only one where doctors and nurses wear Groucho noses, roar with laughter and roll in the aisles during the keynote address.

The convention of The American Association of Therapeutic Humor, which ended on Sunday, featured "Mirth Aid Kits," colored balloons at its check-in table, and offered the "Journal of Nursing Jocularity" among its take-home literature.

But the 500-member group's reason for gathering was no laughing matter. In the nine years the organization has existed, mental and health care professionals have always shared approaches to incorporating humor into their practices, but increasingly, they are sharing scientific data.

"We now have hard-core science that takes us well beyond the psychology of humor," said neurologist Barry Bittman, a pioneer in the relatively new field of psychoneuroimmunology, which studies how emotions affect the immune system.
"This is not just a distraction technique (for patients), we really have the data that shows how the immune system responds," Bittman said.

That is not to say that traditional therapies should be abandoned, experts said. In fact, one reason humor therapy has been slow to catch on is that medical and psychiatric professionals have feared a lack of credibility.

"What we're saying is don't abandon chemotherapy or radiation therapy and don't avoid surgery," Bittman said. "But if you can maintain a positive, upbeat state and can take an active role in your own healing process and if you can incorporate laughter and other positive approaches ... then you have the potential to improve your state of well-being."

Bittman presented new research in which the blood of patients was analyzed before, during and after watching a humorous video. The tests found "significant" boosts to immune function, including higher levels of antibodies and natural killer cells which are the body's most profound defense against aberrant cells such as cancer, he said.
Tests with laboratory rats show people can condition their immune systems to function better by programming the brain with positive messages.

"What we're saying is when you're sitting in the hospital room or receiving chemotherapy don't stare at the four walls. Don't watch the tragedies of the evening news or the conflicts of soap operas," he said. Better that a patient be "in a relaxed meditative state ... so that the right chemistry occurs," he said.

Experts at the conference showed how hospitals can set up "humor carts" and even "humor rooms." Suggested contents included funny movies, books and tapes, and gag toys such as "smile sticks" -- cardboard smiles attached to popsicle sticks that people can hold in front of their faces when they do not feel like smiling for real.
Not only the patients, but the doctors and nurses who deal with them can also benefit from humor, conference leaders said.

"Typically medicine and psychiatry have been serious professions where people have taken themselves very seriously and they should. There's been some anxiety in using humor for fear people won't be taken seriously or that the treatment will be seen as frivolous," said Ed Dunkelblau, an Illinois psychiatrist and incoming president of the association.

Humor helps doctors and nurses cope with horrifying situations and can help boost right brain activity and thus the creative processes, said nurse-humorist Patty Wooten, past president of the organization.

"People do not have to be joke tellers to incorporate humor into their lives. You can surround yourself with humorous things," Wooten said, noting the recent proliferation of nurse and doctor humorists, cartoonists and writers.

She suggested keeping funny toys in your drawer to increase connection with your inner child. "When you're on hold, flip through a cartoon book" to relieve tension. And if you are able, tell a joke. The bottom line, Wooten said, is for everyone to live longer and healthier through humor.
"Halitosis is better than no breath at all," she said.
